headline: Estimating 3D joints from clothed body scans
intro: I adapted my mentor's C# prototype into a Python desktop tool. It estimates joint positions from several views of a clothed body scan and exports the coordinates.
role: I built the Python/VTK version, debugged the coordinate transforms, and added a desktop interface and macOS/Windows packages.

hero.alt: Illustrated synthetic mannequin with pose landmarks and rays converging from several rendered viewpoints.
hero.caption: An illustration of how the tool combines observations from several views. All geometry is synthetic.

metrics.label: Candidate landmarks per image
metrics.note: OpenPose BODY_25; low-confidence detections are filtered.

metrics.label: Desktop platforms
metrics.note: Delivered macOS and Windows application packages.

question.title: Matching each image to its camera
question.text: The lab's method estimates joints by combining pose detections from different views of the same scan. Reproducing it in Python meant keeping the image coordinates, camera transforms, and scan coordinates aligned.

steps.title: Render the scan
steps.text: The tool loads a PLY mesh in VTK, renders the configured views, and saves the camera transform for each image.

steps.title: Trace detections into 3D
steps.text: OpenPose identifies candidate joints in each image. The tool filters low-confidence detections and maps the accepted points back into 3D rays in the scan's coordinate frame.

steps.title: Estimate and export
steps.text: An optimization step combines the rays to estimate joint positions. The desktop interface can process scans in batches, display the joints, and export coordinates.

gallery.alt: Diagram of nine rendered images and an early sequence of eight transforms, highlighting the unpaired repeated endpoint.
gallery.caption: I found nine rendered images paired with only eight stored transforms. Fixing that mismatch restored the alignment.
gallery.credit: Diagram based on a documented development issue. It contains no research output.

finding.title: The finished desktop tool
finding.text: After fixing the alignment, I added controls for selecting batches of scans, progress logs, optional result visualization, and CSV export. I packaged the application for macOS and Windows.

details: My mentor, Byoung-Keon (Daniel) Park, provided the original joint-estimation method and C# prototype. I adapted it to Python and built the research tool around it.
The browser demo uses synthetic data to explain the processing stages. It is separate from the original application and doesn't demonstrate anatomical accuracy.
credits: Research at the University of Michigan Transportation Research Institute, mentored by Byoung-Keon (Daniel) Park.
Pipeline: Python, VTK, OpenPose, SciPy, and Tkinter.
